title: Faço, posso, quero — verbs that break the rules
goal: Conquer the six most common irregular verbs, then use them to ask for help, ask permission and say what you want — politely.
bekal: say the present-tense forms of *fazer*, *poder*, *querer*, *saber*, *ver* and *dizer*
tell *saber*, *poder* and *conhecer* apart — three words that all feel like "can" or "know"
link two verbs with or without a preposition

notes: **Pode ajudar-me?** is the most polite way to ask for help, and it uses the third-person form with no pronoun at all — the Portuguese habit you saw in Unit 1. With a friend, it's *Podes ajudar-me?*

**Sei falar, mas não sei escrever.** Here *saber* means "can" in the sense of **having learned how**: to swim, to drive, to speak Portuguese. Compare *poder*, which means "can" in the sense of **having the chance or permission**: *Não posso ir hoje* (I can't go today — not because I'm unable, but because something's in the way).

**Para si** — the polite form of "for you". In Portugal, *si* is used to address someone politely after a preposition, instead of *você*, which feels too direct: *para si*, *consigo* (with you, polite). This is typical of Portugal and not used in Brazil.
**Fácil demais** — *demais* means "too" and goes **after** the adjective, the opposite of English "too easy". Another form with the same meaning is *demasiado fácil*, which goes in front.
**Demorar** means "to take (time)": *Quanto tempo demora?* = "how long does it take?", *Demora meia hora* = "it takes half an hour". It's used constantly in Portugal.
**Dá-me** — the pronoun *me* hooks on behind the verb again, just like *chamo-me* in Unit 1 and *ajudar-me* in the first line. All the rules are taken apart in Unit 12.

grammars.title: The six most common irregular verbs
body: Notice one helpful pattern: **only the *eu* form is truly surprising**. The other four can almost always be guessed from the infinitive.
after: **Fazer does a lot of jobs.** Besides "to make" and "to do", it's used for weather (*faz frio* — it's cold), for birthdays (*faço trinta anos* — I'm turning thirty), and for asking about jobs (*O que é que fazes?*).

**Querer has its own polite form: *queria*.** It's actually a past-tense form, but it's used exactly like a soft "I'd like": *Queria um café, se faz favor*. Saying *quero* in a café isn't wrong, but *queria* sounds much more polite — and it's what the Portuguese say.

grammars.title: Saber, poder, conhecer — three words for "can" and "know"
body: English uses "can" and "know" for all of these. Portuguese splits them three ways, and the choice isn't flexible.
after: **Saber for facts, conhecer for acquaintance.** *Sei o nome dela* (I know her name) but *Conheço-a* (I know her). Mixing them up sounds instantly odd to Portuguese ears.
*Conhecer* also means "to meet" and "to visit for the first time": *Quero conhecer o Porto* = I want to see Porto (I've never been). Its *eu* form is irregular: **conheço** (koo-NYAY-soo).

grammars.title: Linking two verbs
body: The second verb is always an infinitive. The only thing to learn is which verbs need a preposition in between and which don't.
after: The first four verbs are the ones you'll use most, and luckily they all take **no preposition** — just like English "can" and "must". *Posso ir*, *quero comer*, *sei falar*: a straight line.
*Dever* means "should": *Deves descansar* = you should rest. It's softer than *ter de*, which means "have to" with no choice.

blocks.text: **Pôr is the only Portuguese verb that doesn't end in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*.** It stands alone, with a ^ on its *o* to tell it apart from the preposition *por*. Its *eu* form, *ponho*, is said **POH-nyoo**.

blocks.title: Polite phrases built from these verbs
items: *Pode dizer-me...?* — "Could you tell me...?" The most polite way to ask a stranger something.
*Queria...* — "I'd like...", for ordering anything. *Queria a conta, se faz favor.*
*Sabe onde fica...?* — "Do you know where... is?" Softer than a blunt *Onde fica...?*
*Importa-se de...?* — "Would you mind...?" The most polite way to ask for something that's a bother.
*Posso?* — one word meaning "may I?", for anything: sitting down, getting past, taking something. Extremely useful.
